articles.title: Smartphone ownership at age 12 linked to higher risk of eating disorder symptoms two years later
articles.summary: Adolescents who own a personal smartphone at age 12 face a higher risk of eating disorder symptoms two years later, according to a national study of nearly 9,000 U.S. youth published in JAMA Network Open.

articles.title: Happiness appears to lead to a sense of purpose, but not the other way around, according to new psychology research
articles.summary: People often assume that finding a mission in life leads to greater happiness, but new research suggests the opposite sequence might be more accurate. Feeling good may provide the emotional foundation necessary to pursue long-term life goals.

articles.title: People with depression who use psilocybin are not abandoning standard mental health care, study suggests
articles.summary: People with depression who use psilocybin mushrooms access standard psychiatric care at roughly the same rates as nonusers, a national U.S. survey finds, yet more than half still report an unmet need for mental health treatment.

articles.title: Psychology says frequent worry isn’t a sure sign of shorter nights — it tracks with reporting less sleep, but not what wrist monitors recorded
articles.summary: People who lean toward worry often feel convinced they aren't getting enough sleep. New psychology research in young adults finds that while higher neuroticism tracks with reporting fewer hours, wrist-worn sleep monitors show no shortfall.

articles.title: Scientists used a Harry Potter soundtrack and implanted electrodes to challenge a common assumption about how we hear
articles.summary: Using electrodes implanted inside the brain and a Harry Potter soundtrack, scientists tested how we separate dialogue from music. Their findings in Science Advances suggest the brain may not need special detectors to tell the two apart.

articles.title: Psychology says it’s not the big public shout-out that makes you feel most supported — it’s something far quieter and ordinary
articles.summary: Writing private gratitude letters, posting public shout-outs, and texting someone directly can all lift your mood and ease loneliness. Yet a psychology experiment with 916 college students found that sending a one-to-one thank-you text delivered the biggest boost in feeling connected and supported.

articles.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
articles.summary: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

articles.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals…

articles.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
articles.summary: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up in the brain, the faster depressive symptoms increased, suggesting that mood changes could emerge before cognitive decline.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
articles.summary: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.

articles.title: Form and diversity: How tumor architecture shapes colorectal cancer progression
articles.summary: Tumors are not uniform, as even cancer cells within one patient can display extremely divergent characteristics and behaviors. This diversity, known as tumor heterogeneity, reduces therapeutic efficacy because cells in different states may respond differently to therapeutic interventions.

articles.title: Stronger molecular grip optimizes anticancer drug release

articles.title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease

The surprising discovery could offer an alternative for some patients while reducing reliance on antibiotics.

articles.title: Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong
articles.summary: Loneliness can be surprisingly deadly, with previous research linking it to a roughly 30% increase in the risk of premature death. However, a new study warns that treating loneliness as a medical condition could distract from its deeper social causes. While healthcare professionals can offer support, lasting solutions may require rebuilding communities and fundamentally changing the way people live and work.

articles.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
